rotations.name: Alfalfa
seasons: Alfalfa: all year, cut about 8 to 10 times
rotations.why: Takes 35% of your acres in the suggested plan. In the data it earns about $453 per acre in an average year (the highest profit of the 4 crop rotations), uses about 5.0 acre-feet per acre, and scores 79 for soil.
rotations.evidence: Alfalfa is the thirstiest common crop in central Arizona, often 5 to 6 acre-feet per acre per year. It is a legume, so it adds its own nitrogen.
rotations.benefits: Steady hay income, living roots all year, nitrogen for the next crop, and almost no tillage once planted.
rotations.gaps: We model alfalfa as a 3-year stand averaged per year. We do not model stand decline, pests, or hay quality discounts. In this data its water is a fixed 5.0 acre-feet per acre every year, so it does not change with the weather.
rotations.checkLocally: Ask about your stand age, hay contracts, and whether deficit irrigation in summer makes sense on your soil.

soilReasons.legume: Alfalfa is a legume that fixes nitrogen all year.
soilReasons.livingRoots: A crop is growing in 12 of 12 months (0 bare).
soilReasons.residue: Crop residue rated by crop (cereal straw high, cotton stalks and alfalfa roots medium); bare months count as low cover.
soilReasons.lowTillage: About 2 tillage passes a year in the UA 2025 Pinal budgets (6 passes to establish alfalfa, spread over a 3-year stand).

rotations.name: Cotton then barley
rotations.why: Part of your current plan, but not in the suggested plan at these settings. In the data it loses about $285 per acre in an average year (the lowest profit of the 4 crop rotations), uses about 6.4 acre-feet per acre, and scores 57 for soil.
rotations.evidence: Upland cotton in Pinal County typically uses around 4 acre-feet per acre. Winter barley uses much less because it grows in cool months.
rotations.benefits: Two crops a year, a winter cover of living roots, and residue that protects the soil.
rotations.gaps: Cotton prices and yields vary a lot. We use 20 past years of prices, which may not match the next 20.
rotations.checkLocally: Check gin access, pink bollworm history, and whether your barley can be sold or grazed nearby.

soilReasons.legume: No legume in this rotation, so no nitrogen is fixed.
soilReasons.livingRoots: A crop is growing in 11 of 12 months (1 bare).

soilReasons.lowTillage: About 10.5 tillage passes a year in the UA 2025 Pinal budgets.
soilReasons.diversity: 2 crops in the rotation (barley and cotton).

rotations.name: Durum wheat then sorghum
rotations.why: Not in the suggested plan at these settings. In the data it loses about $85 per acre in an average year (the third-highest profit of the 4 crop rotations), uses about 5.7 acre-feet per acre, and scores 56 for soil.
rotations.evidence: Desert durum grows through the cool season and needs roughly 3 acre-feet per acre. Grain sorghum tolerates heat and uses less water than corn.
rotations.benefits: Uses winter water when evaporation is low, adds crop variety, and returns a lot of residue.
rotations.gaps: Summer sorghum after durum is a tight window. We do not model planting delays or quality premiums for durum.
rotations.checkLocally: Ask about durum contracts and protein premiums, and whether sorghum fits your equipment and harvest timing.

soilReasons.lowTillage: About 11 tillage passes a year in the UA 2025 Pinal budgets.
soilReasons.diversity: 2 crops in the rotation (durum and sorghum).

rotations.name: Barley then fallow
rotations.why: Not in the suggested plan at these settings. In the data it earns about $49 per acre in an average year (the second-highest profit of the 4 crop rotations), uses about 1.9 acre-feet per acre, and scores 42 for soil.
rotations.evidence: Barley grows in the cool season, so it avoids the summer peak in water demand. Leaving fields fallow in summer saves the most water per acre.
rotations.benefits: Low water use, low risk, and some income on land that might otherwise sit idle.
rotations.gaps: Bare summer soil can blow and lose organic matter. We do not model dust control costs.
rotations.checkLocally: Ask about dust control rules for fallow ground and whether a summer cover crop could fit.

rotations.name: Fallow
rotations.why: Takes 65% of your acres in the suggested plan. It uses no water, so it lets the rest of your land get the water it needs.
rotations.evidence: Fallowing is the most common response to water cuts in central Arizona. It costs money for weed and dust control.
rotations.benefits: Frees water for your other fields and is easy to undo next year.
rotations.gaps: The data counts no cost for idle ground. Real costs depend on weeds, dust rules, and land payments.
rotations.checkLocally: Ask about any fallowing programs that pay for conserved water in your district.

soilReasons.lowTillage: About 1 tillage pass a year in the UA 2025 Pinal budgets (one disking for weed control).
soilReasons.diversity: No crop grown, so no diversity.

stressTests.label: 2022: Colorado River water for central Arizona farms cut 65%
2023: no Colorado River water for central Arizona farms
2024: no Colorado River water, record heat

backtest.strategy: Your current plan, cut back to fit your water

assumptions: PARTLY SAMPLE DATA: crop budgets, crop prices still use placeholder or filled-in values. The other inputs are real; Show the math lists every source.
Each of the 20 past years (2005 to 2024) is treated as one possible next year, with its own weather and prices.
Your water budget must hold in every one of those years, including the hottest.
Profits are per acre in 2025 dollars. Water is charged at $70 per acre-foot of applied water; change the price under More options.
Applied water assumes 75% irrigation efficiency unless you change it under More options.
Alfalfa is modeled as a 3-year stand, averaged per year. Pests, diseases, and hay quality are not modeled.
Shares move in 5% steps, so the suggested plan is the best of 10,626 possible mixes.

Soil scores follow the four USDA NRCS soil-health principles (maximize soil cover, maximize continuous living roots, minimize disturbance, maximize biodiversity) plus nitrogen from legumes. An agronomist has not reviewed them yet; check them with a local expert.
